newsitem.title: JORDAN: Rare Arabian antelopes return to Syria.
newsitem.headline: Rare Arabian antelopes return to Syria.

text.p: Eight rare Arabian oryx antelopes, boxed in wooden crates and strapped to the back of a truck, left Jordan on Thursday to be reintroduced to Syria decades after they died out there from overhunting.
The oryx, rescued from the brink of extinction by a captive breeding programme, will be released into Syria's first conservation park, close to the Roman desert city of Palmyra, organisers said.

They were bred in Jordan's Shaumari Nature Reserve, which has reared the endangered antelopes since 1978 and already returned them to the deserts of Oman, Saudi Arabia and Qatar where they once roamed.

"It's exciting when an animal like the oryx...a symbol for all Arabic peoples, can strengthen our friendships in this area," said Khaldoun Kirwan, head of Shaumari's oryx programme, as the antelopes set off for Syria, which has looked on its southern neighbour with mistrust since Jordan's 1994 peace treaty with Israel.
"We hope they'll have no problem at the border," he said of the oryx, who in the wild used to roam over hundreds of thousands of square km of desert.
The white and black oryx, whose long slender horns made them a favourite target for hunters, will be the first animals to be reintroduced to the Talileh park in Syria.
Park official Ahmed Kanana said he hoped they would be joined soon by other species which died out in Syria, including ostrich and wild ass.

Thursday's release of eight oryx to Syria was the prelude to an ambitious project which Jordan's Royal Society for the Conservation of Nature hopes to undertake next year with another of Jordan's neighbours, Israel.

Around 100 oryx are expected to be set free in Wadi Rum and Wadi Araba, straddling the Jordanian-Israeli border. Their movement across what was until 1994 a disputed frontline of the Arab-Israeli conflict will be monitored by satellite tagging.
"Oryx don't recognise borders...they are not part of the dispute," said RSCN chairman Anis Mouasher, when asked if renewed tension between Jordan and Israel could affect cooperation over the project.
But his Syrian colleague Kanana was less keen to draw a line between conservation and politics.
Asked if Syria would be happy to re-stock Talileh with red-necked ostriches given to Jordan last year by Israel, Kanana said they would look for other suppliers.
"We have a deal from Sudan for 30 ostriches," he said.
